paragraphs.heading: Life that buries carbon
paragraphs.text: The biological pump is the set of living processes by which the ocean moves carbon from the air and from land runoff down into its interior and into seafloor sediments. Put simply, life locks carbon away in the deep sea, out of reach of the atmosphere and the land. It is the biological half of a wider marine carbon pump that also has a physical half. It covers two kinds of cycling: the soft-tissue pump, for organic matter made mostly by phytoplankton through photosynthesis, and the carbonate pump, for the calcium carbonate (CaCO₃) that some plankton and mollusks build into shells.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: The ocean helps regulate how much CO₂ is in the air. Each year the pump carries about 10.2 gigatonnes of carbon into the ocean's interior, keeping it away from the atmosphere for several thousand years or more. Without it, atmospheric carbon dioxide would be about 400 ppm higher than it is now.

paragraphs.heading: Step one, the sunlit surface
paragraphs.text: The pump works in three phases. First, in the sunlit surface layer, called the euphotic zone, phytoplankton use carbon dioxide, nitrogen, phosphorus and trace elements such as iron and zinc to make carbohydrates, fats and proteins. Some plankton, such as coccolithophores and foraminifera, also combine calcium with dissolved carbonates to build a protective coat of calcium carbonate.

paragraphs.heading: Step two, the long fall
paragraphs.text: Once carbon is fixed in soft or hard tissue, the organisms either stay near the surface and get recycled, or die and start sinking. On the way down, particles often clump into aggregates, which fall much faster. Clumping gives them a better chance to avoid being eaten or decomposed before they reach the seafloor. Droppings from larger zooplankton such as copepods can join these fast-sinking clumps.

paragraphs.heading: Step three, recycling and storage
paragraphs.text: Carbon that bacteria decompose, during the fall or on the seafloor, is remineralized so it can be used again for new growth. About 1% of the particles leaving the surface make it to the seabed. Those that escape decomposition are buried in sediment, where carbon can stay for millions of years, and this buried carbon is what ultimately lowers CO₂ in the air. Over thousands of years, thermohaline circulation brings dissolved carbon from the deep ocean back to the atmosphere.

paragraphs.heading: Small organisms, big totals
paragraphs.text: Marine phytoplankton fix roughly 50–60 Pg of carbon each year, and ocean production accounts for about half of all carbon fixation on Earth. They do this while making up under 1% of the planet's photosynthetic biomass. Rich upwelling regions produce 2 to 3 times more fixed carbon per area, yet about 80% of the fixing happens in the open ocean, because it covers more than 90% of the ocean's area.
